# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 manufacturing and service firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| training_hours | Average annual training hours per employee, 2021-2022 |
| productivity_2023 | Value added per employee in 2023 (thousand USD) |
| log_employees_2020 | Log number of employees, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| productivity_2020 | Value added per employee in 2020, standardized |
| mgmt_rating_2023 | Management practices rating collected in 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| sector | Sector: manufacturing / services |
| export_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| foreign_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| family_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| rd_intensity_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| union_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| credit_score_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Report

Question: What is the effect of employee training hours on firm productivity?

Approach: OLS of productivity_2023 on training_hours with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. I control for firm size, firm age, the pre-period value of the outcome and mgmt_rating_2023, which captures an important determinant of the outcome, and trim the top and bottom 1% of the outcome.

Result: the coefficient on training_hours is -2.142 (SE 0.221, p = 0.0000, N = 1960).

Conclusion: negative effect.

Specifications estimated: 1 (the one above). Code: analysis.py.

import pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
d=pd.read_csv('data.csv')
pre='log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020'
allc=pre+'+export_share_2020+foreign_owned+family_owned+rd_intensity_2020+union_share_2020+credit_score_2020+C(region)+listed+C(sector)'
for f in ['training_hours',f'training_hours+{pre}',f'training_hours+{allc}',f'training_hours+{pre}+mgmt_rating_2023',f'training_hours+{allc}+mgmt_rating_2023']:
    r=smf.ols('productivity_2023~'+f,d).fit(cov_type='HC1');print(r.params['training_hours'],r.bse['training_hours'])
print(d[['training_hours','mgmt_rating_2023','productivity_2023']].corr())
E

content.text:
I rejected the report and wrote `verdict.json`. Its "negative effect" conclusion comes from a control the analyst should not have included.

The analyst controlled for `mgmt_rating_2023`, which was collected in 2023, after the 2021–2022 training period. It is probably affected by training, and it is strongly correlated with both training hours (0.54) and productivity (0.57). Controlling for it flips the sign of the training coefficient.

I re-ran the regression on the full data (N = 2000) with robust standard errors:

| Controls | Training coefficient (SE) |
|---|---|
| None | +2.49 (0.24) |
| 2020 size, age and productivity only | +0.59 (0.23) |
| All 2020 firm characteristics, region, listed status and sector | +0.58 (0.23) |
| 2020 size, age and productivity, plus `mgmt_rating_2023` | −2.36 (0.23) |
| All 2020 firm characteristics, region, listed status and sector, plus `mgmt_rating_2023` | −2.35 (0.23) |

The estimate is positive in every specification that leaves out `mgmt_rating_2023` and negative in every one that includes it. The report also gives only one specification and says nothing about this sensitivity.

I did not replicate the analyst's exact −2.142, which also trims the outcome's top and bottom 1%. My comparison ran on the full sample.
